questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish a sustaining program's roadmap from the first-program roadmap covered in Data Governance Foundations?
options: The first roadmap is a mostly linear sequence to prove the program should exist; a sustaining roadmap is a backlog of competing initiatives re-sorted on a cadence
A sustaining roadmap is always exactly 12 months long, same as the first one
They are identical documents with no meaningful difference
A sustaining roadmap has no owners or milestones at all
questions.explain: Foundations' roadmap is linear because phases depend on each other; a sustaining program instead manages a backlog of candidate work competing for limited capacity.

questions.q: In the now/next/later horizon structure, what distinguishes 'Now' from 'Next'?
options: 'Next' work always has a firmer date commitment than 'Now' work
'Now' and 'Next' are the same thing, just different labels
'Now' work is committed this quarter with a named owner and milestone; 'Next' is likely but not yet committed
'Now' refers only to work finished last year
questions.explain: Now is committed, disciplined work; Next is scoped and likely but commitment only happens once it moves into Now.

questions.q: Why are 'Later' items described loosely on purpose?
options: Because 'Later' items are never real candidates, just filler
So the roadmap doesn't pretend to know things it doesn't know yet that far out
Because the program has already decided to cancel them
Because loose descriptions are faster to write and that's the only reason
questions.explain: Later items are real candidates, but describing them loosely keeps the roadmap honest about the limits of what can be firmly planned far in advance.

questions.q: Which of the following is named in this lesson as a force that legitimately re-sequences a mature program's roadmap?
options: The council deciding to stop meeting
A maturity assessment exposing a weak dimension
The calendar simply turning over to a new year
A steward successfully completing routine, expected work on schedule
questions.explain: The lesson names four forces: maturity gaps, new domains/regulations, funding changes, and stakeholder turnover — not the mere passage of time.

questions.q: What keeps a multi-year roadmap honest, per this lesson?
options: Revisiting every horizon on a fixed cadence and showing what actually moved to done, not just what's planned next
Hiding the roadmap from the governance council to avoid scrutiny
Adding new items every quarter but never removing or closing any
Committing firm dates two years out and never revising them
questions.explain: A roadmap that only adds items and never shows completed, retired, or re-ranked work is a wish list rather than a credible plan.
